title: Kibbeh bil sanieh
subtitle: Levantine baked lamb and bulgur cake
excerpt: Kibbeh bil sanieh is the baked oven version of kibbeh: two layers of spiced lamb and bulgur enclosing a filling of slow-cooked onion, pine nuts, and aromatic meat. Cut into diamond shapes and baked until the top crust is golden and crisp, it is one of the great dishes of the Levantine table.
sourceNotes: Kibbeh is the national dish of Lebanon and Syria and appears in many forms. Bil sanieh means 'in the tray'; this is the baked form, as opposed to kibbeh nayeh (raw), kibbeh maqli (fried), or kibbeh arnabiyye (in a yoghurt broth).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well after baking. Cut into portions, cool fully, and freeze. Reheat from frozen in a 180 C oven.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble up to a day ahead, refrigerate unbaked, and bake when needed. Add 5 minutes to the baking time.

content.text: Kibbeh bil sanieh is the kind of dish that takes time to make and rewards every minute of it. The outer layer is kibbeh: minced lamb blended with fine bulgur until the mixture is almost pasty and smooth. It encases a filling of caramelised onion, coarsely minced lamb, pine nuts, and allspice.
Pressed into a tin, the top is scored into diamonds and baked until golden. The finished dish cuts cleanly, holds its shape on the plate, and has a firm outer crust and a rich, aromatic interior.
Fine bulgur is essential for the outer layer; coarse bulgur will not bind properly. Soak it briefly in cold water and squeeze it very dry before mixing.

items.prepNote: soaked in cold water for 20 minutes, squeezed very dry
to brush the top before baking

content.text: Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and cook slowly for 15 to 20 minutes until caramelised. Add the coarsely minced lamb and cook, breaking it up, for 8 minutes until browned. Stir in the allspice, salt, and toasted pine nuts. Set aside to cool.

Squeeze the soaked bulgur as dry as possible. Combine with the lean lamb mince, grated onion, allspice, cinnamon, and salt. Work the mixture together by hand or in a food processor until it is very smooth and almost paste-like, about 3 to 4 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 200 C. Oil a 30 x 20 cm baking tin. Press half the kibbeh mixture in an even 1 cm layer across the base. Spread the cooled filling evenly over it. Press the remaining kibbeh mixture in an even layer on top; wet hands help prevent sticking. Using a knife, score the top into diamond shapes. Brush generously with olive oil. Bake for 45 to 50 minutes until the top is deep golden. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting along the scored lines and serving.

rows.fix: Add a tablespoon of cold water to the kibbeh mixture and knead until pliable. Wet hands also help when pressing into the tin.

rows.symptom: Kibbeh layers not holding together when cut
rows.fix: Bake until fully golden and firm. Make sure the filling is cool and fairly dry before adding.

rows.cause: Not enough oil or oven too low
rows.fix: Brush the surface generously with oil before baking. Use the middle to upper shelf.

content.text: Replace the pine nuts with walnuts or leave them out entirely. Some versions include a small handful of raisins in the filling for a sweet note. Serve with a simple fattoush salad and plain yoghurt.

Assemble the entire kibbeh up to 24 hours ahead, then cover and refrigerate. Bake straight from the fridge, adding 5 to 8 minutes to the baking time. Leftovers keep for 2 days and reheat well in the oven.

Kibbeh bil sanieh is the centrepiece of the Levantine table. It appears at Sunday family meals, at weddings, and whenever a large group needs feeding. In Lebanon and Syria it is considered a mark of a skilled home cook. The scoring pattern and the gloss of the olive oil on top are what the dish looks like when it is done properly.
